::: {.lead}
Describe one observation, with its history nested inside, and relflow learns
the encodings, the context, and the predictions from the rows themselves. No
feature pipeline, no fixed-width table, no second path for serving.
:::

::: {.home-actions}
[Build your first model →](learn/your-first-model.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[See what it automates](learn/featureless-models.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary}
:::

## Three fields are a model

::: {.column-screen-inset-right}
::: {.grid .home-code}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-5}
A payment has an amount, a merchant, and a dispute outcome learned later:

```yaml
amount: 84.50
merchant: North Market
disputed: false
```

The merchant vocabulary, the amount scale, the training loop, early stopping,
and the best checkpoint are all handled inside one call. When the question
grows, put the payment last in a `trxns` sequence after the account's earlier
activity. Every transaction keeps its booking time, amount, and merchant
together, and each one gets its own dispute prediction from the shared
context.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-7}
Name the fields, mark the outcome, and train:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    amount=rf.Number,
    merchant=rf.Category,
    disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=20)
```
:::

:::
:::

## What relflow promises

::: {.column-screen-inset-right}
::: {.grid .home-promises}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### No feature pipeline

Vocabularies and normalizers are learned during training and saved inside the
model, and sequence widths follow each batch. The same record layout trains,
scores, and serves. There is nothing to fit offline, rerun before scoring, or
keep in sync.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Model the records as they are

Transactions inside accounts, line items inside transactions, a withdrawal
history beside a payment history. Nested rows are the input, and attention
learns which fields and which events matter together instead of someone
guessing which summaries to compute.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### A target at any depth

Put `mask=True` on a field anywhere in the tree and it becomes a supervised
target that never leaks into the input. Predict a label for every transaction,
a loss for the whole account, or both at once from one model.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Vocabularies that grow while you train

There is no label count to guess. New merchants are admitted before the batch
that introduces them, storage grows in place, and training continues, on one
device or across a distributed run.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Learn before the labels arrive

Hide sampled values and let the model reconstruct them from the rest of the
history, then adapt the same model to the outcome once labels exist. Export
its learned context as vectors for any other predictor.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Change a trained model without starting over

Add a target, drop an input, or extend a branch on a model that has already
learned. State that still fits is kept, and the mutation proofs record exactly
what survives each edit.
:::

:::
:::

Each promise has receipts. The [proofs](proofs.qmd) are small recorded
experiments on the mechanisms behind them: what the architecture can learn,
where it loses information, and the controls that tell the two apart.

## The pipeline you no longer build

::: {.column-screen-inset-right}
```{typst}
//| fig-cap: "A feature pipeline maintains jobs, a fixed-width table, and serving features. A relflow schema reads nested records and learns its own encodings."
//| fig-alt: "Two lanes. The feature pipeline lane runs from source tables through feature jobs that aggregate, encode, and scale, to a fixed-width feature table, a model, and a second set of serving features. The relflow lane runs from nested source records through a schema of fields, branches, and targets to a model that learns vocabularies, normalizers, and context, then to predictions on the same records with labels omitted."
#flow(
  (title: "Feature pipeline", steps: (
    step("Source tables", note: "Transactions, accounts"),
    step("Feature jobs", kind: "target", note: "Aggregate, encode, scale. Rerun before every training and scoring run."),
    step("Feature table", kind: "target", note: "One fixed-width row per entity"),
    step("Model"),
    step("Serving features", kind: "target", note: "A second pipeline kept in sync"),
  )),
  (title: "relflow", steps: (
    step("Source records", note: "Nested rows as stored"),
    step("Schema", kind: "branch", note: "Fields, branches, targets"),
    step("Model", kind: "root", note: "Learns vocabularies, normalizers, and context"),
    step("Predictions", note: "Same records, labels omitted"),
  )),
)
```
:::

[Featureless models](learn/featureless-models.qmd) goes through each pipeline
step and what replaces it, what remains your work, and how to compare the
result with an aggregate-feature baseline.

## Learn in order

Each page builds on the one before it and ends with the next step.

1. [Your first model](learn/your-first-model.qmd): define three fields, train, and predict.
2. [Add transaction history](learn/add-transaction-history.qmd): put the payment and its predecessors in one `trxns` branch and predict a dispute for each.
3. [Featureless models](learn/featureless-models.qmd): see what the two models did without a feature pipeline.
4. [Prepare observations](learn/prepare-observations.qmd): decision times, label windows, ordering, and binding.
5. [Train and save](learn/train-and-save.qmd): the options that matter on a first run, and the artifact.
6. [Read predictions](learn/read-predictions.qmd): find each probability and keep the identifiers you need.
7. [Evaluation](learn/evaluation.qmd): compare with the existing review process before adding more.

Then extend the same model, in this order:

| Business question | What the example adds |
| --- | --- |
| [Will this merchant be paid again?](learn/profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd) | Payment channels, account profile context, and a second outcome learned from the same history. |
| [Which transactions and accounts need attention?](learn/nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd) | Line items inside transactions, a separate withdrawal history, and a future account-loss target alongside transaction disputes. |
| [Can unlabeled activity help?](learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) | Reconstruction of hidden historical fields before adapting to an outcome. |
| [Can other predictors reuse the context?](learn/reusable-representations.qmd) | Frozen transaction-history representations evaluated on separate tasks. |
| [Where else does this pattern apply?](learn/other-domains-and-outcomes.qmd) | Purchase histories for retention, followed by other related-record applications. |

The examples use payments and accounts. The same field and branch definitions
work with other kinds of tabular and nested records.
